whyCorrect: Find the subject and the verb already in the sentence: "its merchants exported cotton, silk, and fruit." The blank follows "and," so it has to be a second verb joined to "exported" in a compound predicate. Only "imported" is a finite past-tense verb that matches "exported" and gives the clause a complete second action.

whyWrong.A: "importing" is a participle, not a finite verb, so it cannot pair with "exported" across the conjunction; the clause would be left with a dangling modifier and no second predicate.
whyWrong.B: "having imported" is a perfect participle phrase, which again supplies no finite verb and also wrongly implies the importing happened before the exporting.
whyWrong.C: "to import" is an infinitive, which would turn the second half into a purpose phrase rather than a parallel action, leaving "and" joining a verb to a non-verb.

commonMistakes: Students see "and" and assume any -ing or to- form will do, without checking that a compound predicate needs two verbs in the same finite form.
tips: When a blank follows "and" in a sentence that already has one main verb, test whether the choice could stand alone as that verb with the same subject.

whyCorrect: "a fictionalized account of the lives of the Mirabal sisters" is a nonessential appositive describing the novel, and it already opens with a comma after "Butterflies." A pair of commas has to close as well as open, so the blank needs the closing comma before the main verb "can serve." That leaves the sentence's core intact: the novel can serve as a starting point.

whyWrong.A: Adding "and" makes it look as though "can serve" is a second item in a list, but there is no second subject, so the sentence loses its main clause.
whyWrong.B: "sisters and" both drops the required closing comma and inserts a conjunction with nothing to join.
whyWrong.D: With no punctuation at all, the appositive never closes, so the opening comma is left unpaired and "the Mirabal sisters can serve" reads as the subject of the sentence.

tips: If a descriptive phrase begins with a comma, look for the matching comma before the sentence's main verb.

whyCorrect: The verb here is "allows," and "allow" takes an object followed by an infinitive: allows researchers to do something. "researchers" is that object, so the blank must be "to study." The rest of the sentence, "chemical reactions occurring within molecules," is what they study.

whyWrong.B: "will study" is a finite verb, which would create a second clause with no conjunction or punctuation joining it to "allows researchers."
whyWrong.C: "who study" turns the rest into a relative clause describing which researchers exist, so the technique no longer allows anything to happen.
whyWrong.D: "studying" is a participle; "allows researchers studying chemical reactions" leaves "allows" without the action it permits.

tips: Learn the fixed pattern for verbs like allow, enable, permit, and require: verb + object + "to" + base verb.

whyCorrect: Check both sides of the blank: "many are still well known" is a complete clause, and "Fama Diagne Sène, for example, is a celebrated playwright from Senegal" is another complete clause. Two independent clauses cannot be joined by a comma or by nothing. The colon works because the second clause is an example that illustrates the general claim in the first.

whyWrong.B: "and" without a preceding comma cannot join two independent clauses; a coordinating conjunction here needs a comma in front of it.
whyWrong.C: A comma alone between two independent clauses is a comma splice.
whyWrong.D: With no punctuation the two clauses run together into a fused sentence.

commonMistakes: Students often reject the colon because they think it only introduces lists, but a colon can also introduce an example or explanation that is itself a full sentence.

whyCorrect: Strip the sentence down: the subject is "Her portrait of novelist Zadie Smith" and the verb is "is displayed." Nothing may separate a subject from its verb, and "novelist Zadie Smith" is a title plus a name that reads as one unit. So the blank takes no punctuation at all.

whyWrong.A: A colon must follow a complete clause; "Her portrait of novelist Zadie" is only a noun phrase, and a colon here would also cut the subject off from "is displayed."
whyWrong.B: The comma splits the subject from its verb and falsely signals that "Smith" ends a nonessential element that was never opened.
whyWrong.D: The dash creates the same subject-verb break as the comma, with an unpaired dash standing in the middle of a noun phrase.

tips: When every choice is the same word with different punctuation, find the subject and the main verb first — if the blank sits between them, the answer is usually no punctuation.

whyCorrect: The sentence already has its main verb: the painting "is inspired by the tradition of qinglu shanshui." Everything after the comma is an appositive renaming that tradition, so the blank cannot introduce a second finite verb. "characterized" is a past participle that modifies "painting" — a reduced relative clause meaning "which is characterized by."

whyWrong.B: "is characterized" is a finite verb, so the appositive turns into a second independent clause spliced onto the sentence with only a comma.
whyWrong.C: "has been characterized" has the same problem as B — a finite verb creating a run-on — and adds a perfect tense the sentence never needs.
whyWrong.D: "will be characterized" is both finite, creating the run-on, and future, which contradicts a description of a long-established painting tradition.

commonMistakes: Seeing a noun right before the blank tempts students to add a verb, but here that noun is inside an appositive that already has a complete sentence in front of it.

whyCorrect: The first sentence makes a general claim: elephants ranked higher than crocodiles. The sentence after the blank does not add a new idea — it supplies the exact rankings, third and fifteenth, that back up that claim. A transition signalling that a detail is about to make the previous statement more precise is what fits.

whyWrong.A: "Therefore" marks a conclusion drawn from the previous sentence, but the rankings are the evidence for that sentence, not a result of it.
whyWrong.C: "On the other hand" sets up a contrast, and the two sentences agree completely.
whyWrong.D: "Later" implies a sequence in time, but both sentences describe the same single list from the same study.

tips: When a sentence restates the previous one with numbers or names attached, the transition is almost always one that signals specificity.

whyCorrect: The natural assumption from "Jupiter LVII" is that Eirene is the fifty-seventh closest moon. The middle sentence overturns that: the numerals record naming order, not distance. The blank sits in the sentence that rejects the assumption, so it needs a transition marking that reversal of the expected reading.

whyWrong.A: "moreover" adds a further point in the same direction, but this sentence contradicts the inference a reader would have drawn from the first sentence.
whyWrong.B: "finally" signals the last item in a sequence, and no sequence of steps or items is being listed.
whyWrong.D: "then" indicates time order or a logical consequence; the conclusion here runs against expectation rather than following from it.

commonMistakes: Students place the contrast against the sentence immediately before, but here the transition reverses the expectation set up by the first sentence.

whyCorrect: The first sentence states the rule: debris orbiting outside the Roche limit should clump into a moon. Morgado's team found a ring at 2,500 miles — well outside the 1,100-mile limit — that has stayed a ring anyway. That finding violates the stated expectation, so the blank needs a concessive transition.

whyWrong.A: "likewise" claims the observation parallels the rule, but the observation is the opposite of what the rule predicts.
whyWrong.B: "for example" would make the Quaoar ring an illustration of the rule, when it is a counterexample to it.
whyWrong.C: "fittingly" says the result is what one would expect, which is exactly backwards.

tips: Compare the numbers before choosing: 2,500 miles is outside the 1,100-mile limit, so the ring should have accreted and did not.

whyCorrect: The question asks for a similarity, so the correct sentence must state something both women share. Only this choice puts them in the same category — both devoted their careers to studying living organisms — using the word "Like" to mark the comparison directly.

whyWrong.A: This contrasts their birth years with "but," emphasizing a difference rather than a similarity.
whyWrong.B: This mentions the two fields but never says anything about Rathbun or Snethlage, so it emphasizes nothing about the two scientists.
whyWrong.C: The phrase "by contrast" explicitly frames their research subjects as different, which is the opposite of what the question asks for.

tips: With notes questions, the stem's goal word — here "similarity" — rules out any choice built on but, however, or by contrast.

whyCorrect: "Scope" here means how much work Basquiat produced. Only one note speaks to volume: more than two thousand drawings and paintings. This choice sets Mater against that total with "just one of more than two thousand," which is what makes the size of his output the point of the sentence.

whyWrong.B: It mentions the two-thousand-plus figure but then pivots to the materials of a single painting, so the sentence ends up about Mater's medium rather than the extent of his output.
whyWrong.C: The auction price and the materials say nothing about how many works he made.
whyWrong.D: This is about when the painting was sold and for how much, which measures market value, not the scope of his body of work.

tips: Decide what the goal word measures — here, quantity of output — and keep only the note that reports that quantity.

whyCorrect: The stated goal is to specify the number of gray wolves in Yellowstone, so the sentence has to contain that number. Only this choice reports it: roughly 100 wolves living in the park. Every other choice leaves the count out entirely.

whyWrong.A: It gives the reintroduction year and the park's location but never states how many wolves there are.
whyWrong.B: It also gives no count, and it misreads the notes: 1995 is when wolves were reintroduced, not a year a population was measured.
whyWrong.C: This defines carrying capacity in general terms and never mentions a number of wolves.

commonMistakes: A choice can be accurate to the notes and still fail, because these questions are scored on whether they meet the stated goal.

whyCorrect: The colon signals that what follows explains the blank. What follows is a population rise from about 100 birds to about 1,300 — exactly the outcome the tree planting was meant to produce. So the blank must be a word meaning the approach worked.

whyWrong.B: "disastrous" would require the population to have collapsed, but it rose more than tenfold.
whyWrong.C: "amusing" describes something entertaining and has nothing to do with whether a conservation effort achieved its goal.
whyWrong.D: "costly" might be true of planting 500,000 trees, but the text after the colon reports results, not expense, so it would not be what the colon explains.

tips: When a colon follows the blank, the words after it define the blank — read them first.

whyCorrect: The sentence says Pak earned his place "by producing acclaimed works," and "Now" contrasts him with the earlier writers who built the tradition. Acclaim strengthens and confirms a position, so the blank needs a word meaning he made his place secure.

whyWrong.A: "contemplated" means he thought about his place, which does not follow from having produced acclaimed works.
whyWrong.B: "subverted" means undermined, but nothing in the text suggests he works against the Hawaiian literary tradition.
whyWrong.D: "extricated" means freed himself from it, the opposite of taking a place within the tradition.

commonMistakes: Reading only the blank's sentence hides the logic; the reason for the answer sits in the phrase "by producing acclaimed works."

whyCorrect: The first sentence stretches from Mexico in North America to Colombia in South America to make one point: there are a great many different languages spread across a great deal of territory. The blank then compares that variety to the continents themselves, which are vast. So the blank means very large.

whyWrong.B: "unknown" contradicts the sentence before, which names specific languages and where they are found.
whyWrong.C: "ordinary" ignores the comparison to the continents and drains the point out of the examples.
whyWrong.D: "limited" reverses the passage — the examples are given precisely to show how wide the range is.

tips: The phrase "Much like the continents themselves" tells you the blank must share a quality with continents; size is the obvious one.

whyCorrect: The example given is a well-executed marketing campaign that pushed a novel to fifth-best-selling of 1996. The blank names the general category that campaign belongs to, so it has to be the word for promotional attention. "publicity" is that word.

whyWrong.A: "originality" is a quality of the book's content, not of a marketing campaign.
whyWrong.C: "complexity" also describes the writing itself and is not illustrated by anything in the example.
whyWrong.D: "practicality" does not name what a marketing campaign supplies, and nothing in the text discusses how practical the novel is.

commonMistakes: Students pick a word that sounds like a virtue of good books, but the blank has to be the category the example belongs to.

whyCorrect: The sentence sets up a contrast: some commentators "lauded" the blogs, while the observers in the blank "countered" with a warning about polarization. "less" plus the blank has to describe the second group as having less of whatever the first group had, and what the first group had was optimism. "sanguine" means cheerfully optimistic, so "less sanguine observers" are the ones who saw the problem.

whyWrong.A: "recalcitrant" means stubbornly uncooperative; "less recalcitrant" would make the critics more agreeable, which contradicts the fact that they are objecting.
whyWrong.B: "earnest" means sincere, and nothing suggests the critics are less serious than the praisers — the contrast is about how positive each group is.
whyWrong.D: "misanthropic" means hating people in general; "less misanthropic" would describe the critics as kinder, the opposite of the negative judgment they offer.

tips: When the blank is preceded by "less," first name the quality the opposing side has, then find the word for it.

whyCorrect: Track the text in three moves. Sentence one makes a broad claim: Barragán's career "evolved through distinct phases." Sentence two describes the early phase, traditional Mexican techniques inside Mediterranean designs. Sentence three describes what changed later, an engagement with modernism after travel abroad. That is a general claim, an early approach, then a later shift.

whyWrong.B: The text never identifies a single "primary aesthetic model" he stayed committed to; its whole point is that his approach changed.
whyWrong.C: The two buildings are given as illustrations of two phases, not as famous works contrasted with lesser-known ones, and the text ranks neither by fame.
whyWrong.D: Nothing in the text discusses his heritage as a reason for his career choice or the impact his career had on others.

commonMistakes: Structure questions are decided by the order of moves, so check each part of the choice against the matching part of the text rather than judging the choice as a whole.

whyCorrect: Arnold reports the Times' view — everyone free to look and act as he likes — only to set up his own claim in the second sentence. That claim is about what culture does: it does not accept a person's raw preferences as the standard, it works toward what is genuinely beautiful and brings people to prefer that. The text exists to state that function of culture.

whyWrong.B: The passage assumes there is something "indeed beautiful" but spends its argument on how culture operates, not on defending objectivity in beauty as a thesis.
whyWrong.C: Nothing in the text traces any change over time in how culture is viewed.
whyWrong.D: The foreign criticism of the English is only a set-up for the argument; the text never compares English taste with anyone else's.

tips: When one view is reported and then answered with "But," the writer's purpose lives in the part after "But."

whyCorrect: The question asks only how the two men first met, so find the sentence that says so. The second sentence states they "had met while performing in a 1960 touring production of Lorraine Hansberry's play A Raisin in the Sun." Both were performers in that production.

whyWrong.A: Harrison is mentioned only as the playwright of a work NEC produced; the text never says he introduced anyone.
whyWrong.B: The Great MacDaddy was produced in 1974, seven years after they had already founded NEC together, so it cannot be where they met.
whyWrong.C: NEC's workshops came after the company existed, so they postdate the meeting; the text never puts Hooks and Ward in one together.

commonMistakes: Both wrong choices built on The Great MacDaddy fail on the timeline — check dates whenever a question asks what happened first.

whyCorrect: The narrator says he did not know what the poems meant, "but that didn't matter," and then closes with "It was quiet and soothing." The memory is about how the sound felt, not about content. He also compares his mother's voice to the drawn-out notes of a cello, which reinforces that what stayed with him was the sound itself.

whyWrong.A: His mother recited existing poems by Rumi and Hafez, not made-up stories, and he says he did not understand them, so characters could not be what he liked.
whyWrong.B: The cello comparison describes his mother's voice, not actual music playing in the background.
whyWrong.C: The text says she chanted to him "every night before bedtime," the opposite of not usually chanting at night.

tips: When a passage says a detail "didn't matter," the sentence right after it usually names what did.

whyCorrect: The text says Davis herself had to transcribe the improvised lyrics, listening repeatedly to unclear vinyl to do it. If usable transcriptions had already existed, that labor would have been unnecessary. So the passage implies there were few or no reliable transcriptions available when she started.

whyWrong.A: The text says nothing about the songs' popularity at any point in time.
whyWrong.B: Davis treats both singers' improvisation the same way; the text never ranks one as more innovative than the other.
whyWrong.C: The recordings are described only as unclear, never counted or compared between the two singers.

commonMistakes: "Most strongly suggests" asks what must follow from a stated detail — here, why the work was labor intensive — not what sounds generally plausible about famous musicians.

whyCorrect: Adlhart's claim is narrow: the sponge would be hard to mass-produce. Support has to bear on manufacturing at scale, not on how well the sponge works. The sponge is made mainly of starch and gelatin, so a finding that those two ingredients are hard to obtain in large quantities directly explains why scaling up production would be difficult.

whyWrong.A: The size of the microplastic problem says nothing about whether the sponge can be manufactured in bulk.
whyWrong.B: Easy shipping would help distribution and, if anything, cuts against a claim about production being difficult.
whyWrong.C: Variable absorption across liquids is a limit on performance, not on manufacturing volume; Adlhart is not disputing how well it works.

tips: Match the evidence to the exact claim — a finding that criticizes the sponge in some other way still fails.

whyCorrect: The claim is specifically that the narrator was frightened of the sailor, so the quotation must show fear rather than mere description. This one has the sailor haunting the narrator's dreams in "a thousand forms, and with a thousand diabolical expressions" on stormy nights — an image of terror felt by the narrator himself.

whyWrong.B: It records the sailor's arrival with a sea-chest, a vivid memory but with no emotional reaction from the narrator.
whyWrong.C: It describes the sailor's silent habits and his telescope, which characterizes the sailor without showing how the narrator felt.
whyWrong.D: It reports the sailor's unchanging clothing and drooping hat; the annoyance mentioned belongs to the sailor's hat in the wind, not to the narrator's fear.

commonMistakes: A quotation about a frightening-sounding character is not the same as a quotation showing that the narrator was frightened.

whyCorrect: The hypothesis is comparative: in low visibility, wider-headed fish should detect obstructions less well than narrower-headed fish. Support therefore needs both head types tested under the same conditions, with the wide-headed fish doing worse. This choice tests medium-sized vortices in low visibility and reports the wide-headed anglerfish hitting more obstructions than the narrow-headed smooth-hound.

whyWrong.A: It tests only a wide-headed species, so "more than half" has no narrower-headed comparison to be worse than.
whyWrong.B: Equal collision rates for both head shapes would undercut the hypothesis rather than support it.
whyWrong.D: It compares individuals within one narrow-headed species, which says nothing about wide heads versus narrow heads.

tips: A comparative hypothesis needs a comparative result: two groups, one condition, and a difference in the predicted direction.

whyCorrect: Two pieces of evidence point the same way. The model says an ectotherm's body temperature falls toward ambient, and the halibut is named as an ectotherm. The basking shark data show its temperature also declines as ambient falls, even though it stays 1.0 to 1.5°C above. Both animals' body temperatures therefore track ambient water temperature at least in part.

whyWrong.A: The text gives no data at all on how variable the tuna's or mako's temperature is, so no comparison with the basking shark can be drawn.
whyWrong.C: The basking shark's temperature is explicitly said to decline as ambient falls, so calling it fixed contradicts the data given.
whyWrong.D: It again calls the basking shark fixed, and it claims the whitetip varies while ambient is stable, which the text never reports.

commonMistakes: Staying a constant amount above ambient is not the same as staying at a constant temperature — the offset is fixed, the temperature is not.

whyCorrect: The researchers' point is that climate change moves species out of old ranges and opens up new habitat, so the conditions that make a species "invasive" somewhere are themselves temporary. The conclusion has to follow from that instability, and "invasive" is exactly the label New Zealand applied to the lorikeet. So the classification rests on environmental conditions that may not last.

whyWrong.A: Nothing in the text describes any earlier lorikeet population in New Zealand or its being outcompeted.
whyWrong.B: This reverses the argument by predicting the lorikeet's success regardless of climate change, whereas the point is that changing climate destabilizes the categories.
whyWrong.D: The researchers question the classification scheme generally; the text never singles out the lorikeet as the one case where the distinction fails.

tips: An inference blank must follow from the sentences immediately before it — here, the two sentences about how climate change shifts ranges.

whyCorrect: The tense is set by the end of the same sentence: the exhibition "ran in early 2022," which is finished and in the past. The main verb has to agree with that completed time frame, so the simple past "featured" is correct.

whyWrong.A: "features" is present tense and would describe an exhibition happening now, contradicting the 2022 run.
whyWrong.B: "has been featured" is passive, which makes the gallery the thing being featured rather than the one doing the featuring.
whyWrong.D: "will feature" places the exhibition in the future, which cannot be squared with a run that already ended.

tips: When a sentence names a specific finished time, that phrase — not your sense of the sentence — decides the tense.

whyCorrect: Look past the long interruption for the sentence's real main verb: "scientists ... adapted the test to foreground smell." "adapted" is already the finite verb for "scientists," so the blank cannot supply a second one. "searching" is a participle that modifies "scientists" and explains why they adapted the test.

whyWrong.A: "searched" is a finite past-tense verb, which leaves the sentence with two main verbs for one subject and no conjunction between them.
whyWrong.B: "were searching" is also finite and creates the same double-verb problem.
whyWrong.C: "have searched" is finite as well, and its present-perfect tense clashes with the past-tense "adapted."

tips: Before choosing a verb form, find the main verb the sentence already has — if there is one, the blank needs a modifier, not another verb.

whyCorrect: The main verb of this sentence is "might ... procure," and its subject is "Antiquarians." That means the blank introduces a modifier describing which antiquarians are meant, not a second predicate. "hoping to read one of Suetonius's extant works" is a participial phrase that does exactly that.

whyWrong.A: "hope" is a finite verb, so the sentence would have two main verbs — "hope" and "might procure" — for one subject.
whyWrong.B: "hoped" has the same double-verb problem and adds a past tense that conflicts with "might procure."
whyWrong.D: "have hoped" is finite too, creating the run-on, and the present perfect adds a time frame the sentence never needs.

commonMistakes: The long dash-and-comma interruption hides the main verb; cross it out mentally and the structure becomes obvious.

whyCorrect: Set aside the nonessential clause "which is attached to the calcaneus" and the sentence reads "The extensor digitorum brevis _____ responsibility for extending the middle toes." There is no other verb, so the blank must be the main verb, and the singular subject in a general statement takes "bears."

whyWrong.A: "bearing" is a participle and leaves the sentence with a subject and modifiers but no predicate.
whyWrong.B: "to bear" is an infinitive, which likewise supplies no finite verb for the subject.
whyWrong.D: "having borne" is a perfect participle — still not a main verb — and wrongly puts the muscle's function in the past.

tips: A clause set off by commas is never the main verb; delete it first and see what is left.

whyCorrect: The sentence opens with "Currently" and ends with "where visitors can view" the work on display — both signal an ongoing present situation. The subject "her painting" is singular, so the present-tense verb must be "hangs."

whyWrong.A: "have hung" does not agree with the singular subject "her painting," which requires "has."
whyWrong.C: "hung" is past tense, contradicting "Currently" and the present-tense "can view."
whyWrong.D: "was hanging" places the display in the past as an ongoing former state, again clashing with "Currently."

commonMistakes: Two things are being tested at once here — tense and subject-verb agreement — so check both before settling on a choice.

whyCorrect: The phrase begins with "with," which introduces an absolute phrase, not a clause: "with the ... Theodulf of Orleans map ... being another one." A finite verb cannot follow the noun in a "with" phrase, because that would start a second clause with no conjunction. "being" is the participle that completes the construction.

whyWrong.A: "is" is a finite verb, so "with the map is another one" fuses a full clause onto the sentence after a preposition.
whyWrong.B: "has been" is finite as well and produces the same ungrammatical structure.
whyWrong.D: "was" is finite too, and its past tense also clashes with a map that is currently held at the Vatican Library.

tips: After "with" plus a noun, English uses a participle, not a conjugated verb — "with the door being open," not "with the door is open."

whyCorrect: The sentence before the blank states a general finding: notable variation in how many native trees different areas have. What follows the blank is two specific figures, 54% in one unit and 12% in another, which are an instance of that variation rather than a new point. The transition therefore has to introduce an example of the finding just stated.

whyWrong.A: "As was previously stated" claims the percentages were already given, but they appear here for the first time.
whyWrong.C: "Contrary to this finding" would require the numbers to conflict with the claim of variation; a 54%-to-12% gap confirms it.
whyWrong.D: "Resulting from this conclusion" reverses the logic — the percentages are the evidence behind the conclusion, not something caused by it.

tips: Data that follows a general statement almost always illustrates it, so look for a transition of exemplification before considering contrast.

whyCorrect: The sentence gives instructions in order: "first consider" the 1661 painting, then do the second thing. The blank has to mark the second step in that sequence, and the earlier word "first" is the signal. "next" is the only choice that continues an ordered set of steps.

whyWrong.A: "therefore" makes the second instruction a consequence of the first, but comparing two paintings is a further step, not a result.
whyWrong.B: "still" concedes a point against something previously said, and nothing here is being conceded.
whyWrong.C: "instead" would replace the first instruction with the second, when the sentence asks you to do both.

tips: The word "first" earlier in a sentence is a direct clue that the blank continues a sequence.

whyCorrect: The first sentence states a general principle: energy transfers across trophic levels. What follows the blank walks through plants feeding deer feeding coyotes — a concrete illustration of that principle, not a new or opposing idea. The blank needs a transition that introduces an illustration.

whyWrong.A: "By contrast" requires two things being set against each other, but the food chain described agrees with the principle stated.
whyWrong.B: "Likewise" adds a parallel case alongside a first one, and no first case has been given — only the general rule.
whyWrong.C: "However" signals a reversal, and nothing about the plant-deer-coyote chain contradicts the idea of energy transfer between levels.

commonMistakes: Students reach for a contrast transition when a sentence looks long or detailed; check whether the detail agrees with what came before.

whyCorrect: The goal is narrow: specify the test site's climate. Only one note gives a climate — temperate midlatitude — and only this choice states it. Everything else in the notes is about the study's subject, location, or result.

whyWrong.A: It names the country and what was tested but never says what the climate was.
whyWrong.B: It reports the study's finding, which is a result, not a climate.
whyWrong.D: It mentions "a given climate" without ever specifying which one, so it does not accomplish the stated goal.

tips: When the goal names one piece of information, scan the choices for the note that contains it and ignore how complete the rest of the sentence sounds.

whyCorrect: The goal has two parts: state a generalization and support it. This choice does both — the general claim is that some countries' flags include animal symbols, and the eagle on Kazakhstan's flag is offered as the supporting instance. No other choice pairs a claim with an example of it.

whyWrong.A: It states that many flags carry symbols but then defines vexillology instead of supporting the claim with an example.
whyWrong.B: It gives only the single example, with no generalization for that example to support.
whyWrong.C: It defines vexillology and describes vexillologists' interests, which is not a generalization about symbols on flags at all.

commonMistakes: A two-part goal needs a two-part sentence; a choice that nails one half and drops the other is still wrong.

whyCorrect: The stated goal is to provide a quotation from chapter 17, so the correct sentence must contain quoted words from Boym. This is the only choice with quotation marks around her language, and it correctly frames the quotation with what chapter 17 is about — skeptics' takes on nostalgia.

whyWrong.A: It summarizes what two chapters cover and quotes nothing.
whyWrong.B: It describes the book in general and includes no quotation.
whyWrong.D: It paraphrases chapter 14's subject rather than quoting chapter 17, and its incomplete phrase "in chapter of her book" names no chapter at all.

tips: When the goal says "provide a quotation," eliminate every choice without quotation marks before reading further.

whyCorrect: The colon after the blank explains it: "we will never be able to answer it." A question that can never be answered is one that cannot be settled, so the blank needs a word meaning exactly that. "irresolvable" is that word.

whyWrong.B: "self-contradictory" would mean the question conflicts with itself, but the problem is a lack of evidence about ancient people, not a flaw in the question's logic.
whyWrong.C: "imperative" means urgently necessary, which does not follow from being permanently unanswerable.
whyWrong.D: "unavoidable" describes something that must be faced, not something that cannot be answered.

tips: Cover the choices, predict a word from the clause after the colon, then find the closest match.

whyCorrect: The sentence opens by saying some music has many meanings, and it ends by saying a listener's interpretation is hard to call a misunderstanding. For both halves to hold, Moorman's compositions must accommodate that many readings — the blank means to sustain or allow them. "support as many different interpretations as there are people" is the reading that fits.

whyWrong.A: "refute" would mean the compositions disprove the interpretations, which contradicts the conclusion that listeners' readings are hard to fault.
whyWrong.B: "omit" means to leave out, but the point is that the music takes in many readings, not that it excludes them.
whyWrong.D: "evade" means to avoid, again implying the music escapes interpretation rather than sustaining many.

tips: Read to the end of the sentence: the final clause about listeners not being wrong tells you the blank must be positive toward interpretations.

whyCorrect: The first sentence says a team of both engineers and entomologists ran the study together. The second says this produced a more comprehensive approach than either discipline could have managed alone. The blank names what the two groups did jointly, so it has to mean working together.

whyWrong.A: "skepticism toward" describes doubt about the experts, which would not explain a better combined result.
whyWrong.B: "exaggeration of" makes no sense as a cause of a more comprehensive approach and is not something the text mentions.
whyWrong.C: "distrust among" is actively at odds with a joint effort that outperformed independent work.

commonMistakes: The contrast with "independent efforts" at the end of the sentence is the clue — the blank must be the opposite of working separately.

whyCorrect: The semicolon explains the blank: detailed sets were not common until the 1600s. If audiences before then had only ever seen bare stages, a bare stage would have been the norm for them. That is the contrast with today's theatergoers, who are "surprised" by sparse staging precisely because they are used to elaborate sets.

whyWrong.A: "disliked by" adds a judgment the text never supports; nothing says early audiences objected to plain staging.
whyWrong.B: "confusing to" describes the modern reaction the passage says arises from unfamiliarity, which is the opposite of an audience that knew nothing else.
whyWrong.D: "exciting to" would make plain stages a novelty for early audiences, but they were the ordinary practice of that era.

tips: When the sentence begins with "But," the blank must reverse the state of affairs described just before it — here, modern surprise becomes past normality.

whyCorrect: The second sentence tells you what the relationship is: acclaimed writers "have drawn on these stories" to build their portraits of Hawaii. The blank has to describe modern Hawaiian literature taking its material from those traditional stories, which is what "derived from" means.

whyWrong.A: "brooded on" means dwelt anxiously upon, which is not the same as taking source material from them.
whyWrong.B: "supplanted" means displaced or replaced, the reverse of building on the traditional stories.
whyWrong.C: "anticipated" would put the modern literature before the traditional stories, reversing the chronology.

commonMistakes: The second sentence is doing the defining work here; the blank restates "drawn on" in different words.

whyCorrect: The text does two parallel things: it describes the Hispanic Society of America — when it was founded, what it is devoted to, how large its collection is — and then the Latino Cultural Center, where it is and what it focuses on. Both descriptions center on each institution's subject area. There is no argument or comparison beyond that.

whyWrong.A: Funding is never mentioned; the text says the Hispanic Society acquired objects but not how it paid for them.
whyWrong.C: No historical development is traced, and the text never says why either institution was founded.
whyWrong.D: Only one collection size is given — 18,000 objects — so no contrast between sizes is possible.

tips: For purpose questions, check that every element of the choice actually appears in the text; one invented detail is enough to eliminate it.

whyCorrect: Follow the three moves. Adelaide is named as one city that has installed hardening structures — an example of a location using the approach. The middle sentence lays out how Prosser's team studied it: the Index of Waterbird Community Integrity, sixty-four species, the Chesapeake Bay. The last sentence reports what they concluded. Example, method, finding.

whyWrong.A: No hypothesis is stated anywhere, and the last sentence is a conclusion drawn from the survey, not evidence offered to support a prior prediction.
whyWrong.C: The final sentence is a stated conclusion from the data, not a supposition, and the opening sentence reports a practice rather than making a claim about it.
whyWrong.D: The text never notes the significance or implications of the findings; it stops at what the researchers concluded.

commonMistakes: Structure choices often differ only in their last clause — read all three parts of each option against the matching part of the text.

whyCorrect: The text has two parts and one relationship between them. Van Berlo's meta-analysis established the finding: advergames can hold interest but leave players unable to recall brand information. The rest of the text says that finding "can be explained by" Lang's limited capacity model, because players' cognitive resources go to gameplay first. The main idea is that Lang's model explains van Berlo's result.

whyWrong.B: The text is about recall of information, not about persuading players to buy anything; purchasing is never mentioned.
whyWrong.C: This says advergames can succeed despite Lang's model, but the text uses Lang's model to explain a limitation, and it proposes no balancing solution.
whyWrong.D: It reverses the direction of the argument — Lang's model explains van Berlo's finding, rather than van Berlo's research confirming a conclusion Lang had drawn about video games.

commonMistakes: When a text pairs a finding with a theory, check which one is doing the explaining; swapping them produces a very plausible-sounding wrong answer.

whyCorrect: The last sentence does the work. Mexico City had higher park use (77.6% versus 67.5%) but a much lower share of residents living within a 10-minute walk of a park. Since the city with worse access had more use, closeness cannot be what produced the gap — some other factor must be responsible.

whyWrong.A: The text never questions the survey's accuracy; it takes the reported percentages at face value and reasons from them.
whyWrong.B: No earlier data sources are mentioned; both figures come from this one survey.
whyWrong.C: The text says nothing about what the researchers expected.

tips: When a text rules out one explanation, the point being made is about that explanation's failure, not about the numbers themselves.

whyCorrect: The claim is that Henry does not always comfort Jimmie after a scolding. The quotation must therefore show Henry responding to a disgraced Jimmie with something other than comfort. This one has Henry repudiating Jimmie's behavior, bullying him, and preaching his father's rules back at him — the opposite of consolation.

whyWrong.A: It shows Jimmie's admiration for Henry's work with harnesses and horses, which explains why Jimmie looks up to him, not how Henry responds to him.
whyWrong.B: Here Henry confesses a fault of his own to put himself on equal footing with Jimmie, which is precisely the comforting behavior the claim says he does not always offer.
whyWrong.D: This describes Jimmie withdrawing from Henry when Henry is guilty, so the failure of the relationship runs the wrong way — it is Jimmie's behavior, not Henry's.

commonMistakes: A quotation showing the relationship going badly is not enough; it has to show the specific person named in the claim behaving the specific way described.

whyCorrect: The claim is about the narrator struggling to accept her own race, so the strongest quotation is the one where she rejects her own features outright. Here she calls her life a "black ugly dream" and imagines her "real hair" as long and blonde, treating the hair she actually has as a mistake to be woken up from. That is non-acceptance stated directly by the narrator about herself.

whyWrong.A: It describes the dress and a wish to look like white girls, but the focus is on the garment and Momma's stitching rather than on rejecting her own identity.
whyWrong.B: It imagines strangers apologizing to her for not recognizing her, which is about wanting recognition, not about her race.
whyWrong.D: This is a general statement about Southern Black girls as a group; it does not show the main character's own struggle with self-acceptance.

tips: For evidence questions about a character's inner conflict, prefer the quotation where the character speaks about herself, not about people in general.

whyCorrect: The student's claim has a precise shape: cultured meat may help respond to an expected widespread change in public behavior. Only this quotation describes a future behavioral shift — a growing population eating significantly more meat, driving demand up through the 21st century. That is the change cultured meat could be positioned to meet.

whyWrong.A: Lower water consumption is an environmental advantage of the technology, not a change in what the public does.
whyWrong.B: Variation in meat flavor across species and farming conditions has nothing to do with public behavior changing.
whyWrong.D: This reports what consumers currently believe about packaging, which is a present opinion rather than an expected change in behavior, and it is not about meat consumption.

commonMistakes: Choices that praise cultured meat are tempting, but the claim is specifically about a coming change in behavior — the evidence has to name that change.

whyCorrect: The final sentence points out that most studies on this topic were run in North America at sites resembling one another, while the outlying study was run in Brazil. That is a statement about where the research was done, so the conclusion must be about setting. If the North American sites share characteristics the Brazilian ones do not, the differing result may come from the different environment rather than from an error.

whyWrong.A: Nothing in the text compares measurement precision across studies.
whyWrong.C: The text offers no reason to think the Brazilian team measured the wrong variable; it explains the discrepancy by geography, not by faulty measurement.
whyWrong.D: No actual mercury or carbon values from either study are given, so no such numerical comparison can be drawn.

tips: An inference blank has to be built from the clause right before it — here, the observation that the study sites are geographically clustered and similar.
